newsitem.title: CHINA: China rumoured to push new crackdown on bourses.
newsitem.headline: China rumoured to push new crackdown on bourses.

text.p: China may soon ban several major brokerages from conducting securities trading on their own account and remove its top securities regulator after failing to stop overheating on its stock markets, brokers said on Thursday.
The chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), Zhou Daojiong, was expected to step down soon and an announcement was likely within days, Chinese brokers said.
Zhou, who was appointed in 1995, was expected to be replaced by Zhou Zhengqing, currently chairman of the Securities Commission under the State Council, or cabinet, they said.
However, this could be a temporary assignment for Zhou Zhengqing since the post of head of the CSRC is subordinate to his current position, Beijing sources said.
Regulators have been unhappy with the inability of securities authorities to rein in China's surging stock markets in Shanghai and in southern Shenzhen, brokerage sources said.

A previous attempt to end a bull run when the People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, issued a harshly worded editorial warning of overheating and a market crash sent prices tumbling and dampened market sentiment for weeks.

However, China's stock indices have risen more than 50 percent since the start of this year despite Beijing's repeated calls for the markets to cool down and brokers said the government would have to come up with more innovative ways if it hopes to succeed in cooling the markets again.
CSRC officials have declined to comment on the reports.
Brokers said Zhou Daojiong had reached retirement age and that his removal had been under discussion for months.
Other reports circulating among brokers were that the head of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, Yang Xianghai, and his Shenzhen counterpart, Zhuang Xinyi, would be replaced.

In another move to cool the markets, at least four brokerages, including Shenyin & Wanguo Securities, China's largest, would be barred from conducting trading for themselves after irregularities, brokers said.
Asked if Shenyin & Wanguo was among those to be punished, one company official company said: "Yes, this is the case."
Officials at Shenzhen-based J&A Securities and Guangfa Securities confirmed they too would be similarly disciplined.
One official of Guangfa said the brokerage house expected to be told to stop trading on its own account, but said he did not know how long the sanctions would be imposed.
The brokerage houses to be punished would also lose their rights to issue bonds in the primary market, he said.
Shanghai-based Haitong Securities was also believed to be facing similar sanctions along with several other, smaller houses, brokers said.
There was expected to be a reshuffle in the leadership of the brokerages but details were not yet available, brokers said.
The move does not appear to affect the brokers' ability to trade on behalf of their clients.
Several listed firms could be punished for irregularities, including trading their own shares, brokers said.
"The central government seems more determined than ever before to expand and develop the markets, but only on the basis of good supervision and regulation," one broker said.
